doc.title: Putter Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 27, 2024

title: Stamina, first gig at 13 and playing by ear in the footsteps of brother Carson
summary: Smith describes playing without amps, tape and blisters, his first gig at 13, and his bassist brother Carson. He played along with Carson's records by ear on a half-size, three-string bass.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: The physicality of playing the bass — did it take you some time as a young man to, I don’t know, build up the stamina, the muscles, to play the acoustic bass?

Well yeah. When I started, my first professional gig was 1954. Back then there were no amps and all bass players carried a packet — a little thing of white adhesive tape like present day congolera players have. You know you just tape your fingers And bleeding and blisters were — that was part of it. And you were digging in. You couldn’t just turn the volume up you had to dig in you know and generally it was painful for a few minutes

and then you went numb and — but that was the way it was done in those days. The physical part of playing the bass, yes it is a very physical instrument and I was fortunate that I was surrounded by very good bass players and began studying classically when I was about 15. And my first gig was when I was 13 and it was pure guts. I mean just — I don’t know do you know that my brother is a famous bass player? Carson Smith?
I do. As a matter of fact —
Oh yeah that looks like him yeah. That’s very similar to my brother, yeah. Hey Carson.
That’s his gig with Chico Hamilton.

That’s right. I know all those guys. I used to see all those guys I was, like I say I was 13 when I started playing. I was about that age when he was working with them. Ten years difference. And let’s see where was I going with that?
You were talking about playing without amps and the physicality of it.

Oh yeah well the first gig somebody came up — my brother was famous in jazz at that time. And I was in around ninth grade or tenth grade. And somebody came up to me and said, “Are you Carson’s brother?” I said, “Yeah, yeah.” He says, “You play the bass?” I go, “Yeah,” I lied. And I used to — he had left a half-sized bass there that I used to fool around with and then when his records came out with Chet Baker and Gerry Mulligan I used to play along with those, not knowing anything. All I knew was how it was supposed to sound. And I was playing completely by ear not knowing anything.
Sorry for the interruption — That term, “not knowing anything” I think is an important thing to say. Let me see if I can pin you down. What do you mean by that? “Not knowing anything?”

Names of the notes, keys, chord changes, the proper way to hold the instrument. You know I just — it was pure — what is it, visceral playing. And I knew what it was supposed to sound like and from playing along with the records I — but there was no caution at all, it was just bang — you know, bang bang. And so I took the gig, they picked it up — they didn’t call them “gigs” then. That word came in a few years later. And I only had three strings on the bass and I don’t really even remember which ones they were, but I knew how to “get down” as they say, you know, and I just got down and within a very short time I was working all the time and consequently missed out on all the social events of my high school because I was always working and all that stuff. And at the time I felt really great about it, but now I kind of wish I had learned to dance with all the lovely young girls in my, you know — we all have regrets, right?
